Eldest
EL-dest
a.
Superlative of old, from Anglo-Saxon ieldesta. Webster 1828: oldest; that was born before others. In two narratives the eldest is where a search or a conviction begins, and in both the order is significant.

Biblical Definition

Joseph’s steward searches the sacks in a sequence that builds suspense and proves a point: he searched, and began at the eldest, and left at the youngest: and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack (Genesis 44:12). Ten sacks are opened and cleared before the last one damns the brother Jacob could least spare, and the whole test is designed to see whether these men will now abandon a favoured younger son as they once abandoned Joseph. They do not; Judah offers himself instead. John records a different search conducted by conscience, and it moves in the same direction: they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst (John 8:9). The oldest went first, having most to remember. Samuel records the three eldest sons of Jesse following Saul to the battle while the youngest kept sheep (1 Samuel 17:13), and Job’s children were feasting in their eldest brother’s house when the messengers came (Job 1:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ELDEST as oldest; most advanced in age; that was born before others; and of a family, the first-born.

expand to see more

ELDEST, a. — Oldest; most advanced in age; that was born before others.

ELDER, a. — Older; having lived a longer time; prior in origin.

ELDER, n. — One who is older; an officer in the church, a presbyter.

ELDERSHIP, n. — Seniority; also the office of an elder.

Anglo-Saxon ieldesta, superlative of eald, old.

Key Scripture

Genesis 44:12 — "And he searched, and began at the eldest, and left at the youngest: and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack."

John 8:9 — "And they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst."

1 Samuel 17:13 — "And the three eldest sons of Jesse went and followed Saul to the battle: and the names of his three sons that went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, and next unto him Abinadab, and the third Shammah."

Job 1:13 — "And there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house:"

Modern Corruption

John 8:9 shows conscience working without a word of accusation from Christ, which the popular use of the passage as a rule against all moral judgment entirely inverts.

expand to see more

He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her is probably the most cited verse in the modern world and one of the least understood. It is not a prohibition of moral judgment: the same Christ, in the same paragraph, tells the woman go, and sin no more — naming what she had done as sin and requiring it to stop. What He refuses is the right of these particular men, who had brought the woman without the man and used her as bait for a trap, to execute a sentence they had no standing to execute. Conscience did the rest, and it began at the eldest, who had most to remember. To read the verse as forbidding all moral assessment one must delete the last sentence of the story, and it is generally deleted.

Genesis 44 is worth reading as the test it is. Joseph places his cup in Benjamin’s sack and has the search begin at the eldest, so that ten brothers are cleared in turn and the youngest — the son of Rachel, his father’s favourite, exactly the position Joseph himself had occupied — is left holding the evidence. The brothers are being offered the same choice they made years earlier, with every incentive to take it: they could leave Benjamin and go home. Instead they rend their clothes and return, and Judah, who had proposed selling Joseph, offers himself as bondman in the boy’s place. That is what genuine repentance looks like in Scripture: not remorse expressed, but the same temptation refused in the same circumstances.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gadol (H1419), great, and so eldest; bekor (H1060), firstborn; Greek presbuteros (G4245), older, an elder.

expand to see more

Hebrew gadol (H1419) — great, and by extension the eldest; began at the eldest (Genesis 44:12).

Hebrew bekor (H1060) — the firstborn, with the rights of the birthright; Eliab in 1 Samuel 17:13.

Greek presbuteros (G4245) — older, elder; beginning at the eldest (John 8:9) and the church office of elder.

Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience, joint-knowledge; what convicted the accusers (John 8:9).

Hebrew qaton (H6996) — small, young, least; left at the youngest (Genesis 44:12).

Usage

"He searched, and began at the eldest, and left at the youngest (Genesis 44:12) — a sequence designed to isolate the favoured son."

"Being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest (John 8:9) — the oldest had most to remember."

"The three eldest sons of Jesse went and followed Saul to the battle (1 Samuel 17:13) — and the youngest kept sheep."
